 Highlights 
 Tuas' Singapore mobile arm Simba must answer the regulator's show cause notice by Monday, and the shares remain under pressure. As Tuas continues operating within the ASX 300 , growing attention is also being directed towards ASX Communication Stocks as companies across the sector navigate changing market conditions.
 For readers following the ASX All Ords and ASX news today, Tuas remains among the stocks to watch.
 The annual meeting at the end of the month will be the earliest formal gathering of owners since the notice landed.

 has entered the final days before its Singapore mobile operator Simba must reply to the Infocomm Media Development Authority's show cause notice, with the response due on Monday and the shares still drifting lower.
 The deadline in focus
 The notice reached Simba on a Friday evening in late October, Sydney time, and Tuas disclosed it to the market the following Monday morning. The regulator set the middle of November as the date by which Simba must explain why findings should not be made against it.
 Simba has said it intends to respond before the deadline. Beyond that commitment, Tuas has said it will not comment while the matter is before the regulator, which leaves the market with little to work from in the run-up to Monday.
 What Simba is being asked to answer
 As summarised by Tuas, the notice sets out a series of allegations covering several years of network operations:
 running older and newer mobile technologies together on a band licensed for the latest generation only, across many sites
 using a separate band at a large number of sites without authorisation
 that both practices were intentional and approved at a senior level
 switching on indoor radio equipment at a small number of locations before approval
 incomplete compliance with an order to produce documents
 wider concerns about governance and compliance culture
 The regulator has stressed that it has made no findings at this stage.
 What is at stake
 The range of possible outcomes is wide. At the milder end sit compliance orders and financial penalties, which are capped at the greater of a fixed sum or a share of annual turnover in the affected part of the business. At the harsher end, the regulator could suspend or cancel spectrum rights, in whole or in part, or shorten or cancel the operating licence itself.
 How the shares have tracked
 The earliest reaction in late October was severe, with the stock sliding sharply in a single session on very heavy volume, and further falls followed after the regulator publicly set out its concerns. Since then, the shares have struggled to find a floor.
 Tuesday's slip was small in size but telling in context. With the benchmark rising strongly and most sectors in positive territory, Tuas was among the handful of names to finish lower, suggesting few traders are willing to take a position ahead of Monday's filing.
 A difficult year before the notice
 The probe follows a series of setbacks in Singapore. Earlier this year, Tuas and its counterparty called off a planned deal for a rival Singapore mobile business owned by Keppel after the regulator paused its review amid concerns over spectrum use and unmet approval conditions. That collapse removed the company's main path to scale in the city-state.
 What happens after Monday
 Lodging a response does not end the process. The regulator will assess the submission, may seek more information and will then decide whether to make findings and, if so, what action to take. No timetable has been given for that decision.
 Whether Tuas discloses any of the content of Simba's reply is uncertain. Companies in regulatory proceedings often say little until there is an outcome, although continuous disclosure rules would require an update if anything material emerges.
 It is also possible the regulator will engage with Simba on remedies before deciding on any formal action. Negotiated outcomes, such as enforceable undertakings to tighten compliance, are sometimes used in licensing disputes, and they can give a company a clearer path forward than a drawn-out contest.
 The annual meeting at month's end
 Tuas has called its annual meeting for the last day of November at a hotel in Sydney. The formal agenda is short, covering the remuneration report and the re-election of a single board member whose background includes many years at a large Australian telco.
 The notice contains a small inconsistency on the proxy deadline, with the notice and the proxy form giving different days. Owners planning to vote by proxy may want to lodge early to avoid any confusion.
 Where Tuas sits in the market
 The slide has left Tuas a much smaller company than it was at the start of the year, though it remains comfortably inside the wider All Ordinaries . Among ASX Communication Stocks , it is unusual in drawing almost all of its revenue from outside Australia, which ties its fortunes closely to a single foreign regulator.
 Questions owners are likely to raise
 what internal reviews have been carried out on spectrum practices
 whether governance and compliance staffing has been strengthened
 how customer growth and network performance have tracked since the notice
 whether lenders or suppliers have raised concerns
 Management may decline to discuss the regulatory matter in detail, but the tone of its answers on operations will still be closely read.
 Why the market stays cautious
 Regulatory cases rarely move quickly, and uncertainty tends to be priced harshly. Until the regulator signals the form of its decision, the stock is likely to trade on headlines from Singapore rather than on subscriber numbers or margins. A clearly financial outcome could ease the pressure; any move against spectrum rights would likely deepen it.
 The answer for now
 Yes, the shares are still sliding, if more gently than in late October, as the market waits for Simba's reply. Monday's filing is a milestone, but not the finish line. The decisive moment will be the regulator's eventual response, and until then Tuas is likely to remain among the most closely watched, and most volatile, names in the local telco sector.

 Simba's response to the show cause notice is due on Monday, and the company has said it intends to meet that deadline.

 No, the regulator has stressed that no findings have been made and no decision on action has been taken.
